title: Tool Design & MCP
goal: Pick the cheapest layer that fixes a routing, error, selection, or scope failure, and name the distractors the exam dresses up as architecture.

steps.title: Two tools, one word: content
steps.lead: Production first. A support agent sends "analyze the uploaded quarterly report" to the web-search agent 45% of the time. The web-search agent has `analyze_content`, described as "analyzes content and extracts key information". The document agent has `analyze_document`, described as "analyzes documents and extracts key information".
points: Nothing in the wiring is broken. The model is choosing from the only signal it has: the tool description.
Both descriptions claim the same verb on nearly the same object. That overlap is the bug.
Misrouting fix order: descriptions, then few-shot examples, then merge tools, then a routing classifier. That last one is wrong.
steps.takeaway: A tool description is not documentation. It is the selection criteria the model routes on.

steps.title: Which fix actually removes the overlap?
steps.lead: You are reviewing the routing failure above and must choose a remediation.

ask.q: Production logs show requests like "analyze the uploaded quarterly report" are routed to the web-search agent 45% of the time instead of the document analysis agent. `analyze_content` is described as "analyzes content and extracts key information"; `analyze_document` as "analyzes documents and extracts key information." Which approach is most effective?
options: Add a pre-routing classifier that detects whether the user refers to uploaded files or web content before the coordinator delegates.
Add few-shot examples to the coordinator prompt showing correct routing for uploaded files versus web pages.
Expand only the document analysis tool description with usage examples, leaving the web-search tool unchanged.
Rename the web-search tool to `extract_web_results` and rewrite its description as "processes and returns information retrieved from web search and URLs."
ask.why: Tool names and descriptions are the selection mechanism, so removing the semantic overlap between the two tools fixes the root cause. A pre-routing classifier adds a component that masks the ambiguity instead of resolving it, few-shot examples treat the symptom at a token cost on every call, and expanding only one of the two descriptions leaves the other still claiming to analyze content.

steps.takeaway: When two descriptions collide, rewrite the text before you add infrastructure.

steps.title: Write descriptions like selection criteria
steps.lead: The exam keeps ranking the layers: description text is the cheapest layer that reaches the root cause. Make it do its job before you reach for anything else.
points: State purpose, input format, output format, edge cases, and the explicit boundary against similar tools.
A description containing "or" or "depending on" is two tools wearing one name.
Split when parameters carry interdependent constraints, or when each action type needs a different required field.
Closed sets belong in the schema as `enum` values, for example `knowledge_base`, `billing_records`, `support_tickets`.
Never bury a format hint in a parameter name. Put it in the description and the schema.
steps.takeaway: If the description contains an or, the tool is doing two jobs.

steps.title: One refund tool, four behaviours
steps.lead: A single tool is trying to cover four different actions, and the parameter sets do not agree.

ask.q: A single `manage_refund` tool is described as "processes refunds, partial refunds, store credits, or exchanges depending on policy and customer status." Output shapes are inconsistent in production and the agent frequently sends the wrong parameter set. Which approach is most effective?
options: Split it into purpose-specific tools with tight contracts: `issue_full_refund`, `issue_partial_refund`, `issue_store_credit`, `process_exchange`.
Keep one tool but add a `mode` enum parameter listing the four behaviours.
Rename the tool to `refund_processor` and expand its description to explain each mode.
Add few-shot examples to the system prompt showing each mode in use.
ask.why: A description with "or" or "depending on" cannot be disambiguated at runtime, and purpose-specific tools with typed contracts make each parameter set unambiguous. A mode enum and a rename both leave the over-broad contract intact, and few-shot examples treat the symptom rather than the contract.

steps.takeaway: Rename and enum are the same non-fix. Description is weaker than contract.

steps.title: What the model actually sees
steps.lead: Here is the whole contract. Everything else about your tool is invisible to the model.
points: `name` and `description` route the call. `input_schema` constrains the arguments.
The result, including its error shape, drives the next step.
After clean descriptions, misrouting can still persist. Then audit the system prompt for keyword-sensitive instructions that override them.
steps.caption: Description routes, schema constrains, result decides.
steps.takeaway: Route with the description, constrain with the schema.

steps.title: An empty array is not an error
steps.lead: `get_customer` returns an empty array in two situations: no customer matches the search, and the customer database is unreachable. The agent retries both, then tells the user "customer not found".
points: A valid empty result is information. Return `isError: false` with an empty array and let the agent report that it found nothing.
A genuine access failure must not be able to masquerade as an empty result. This is the canonical trap in this task.
Returning an empty array while the backend is down converts I could not search into I searched and there is nothing.
steps.takeaway: `isError: true` means the tool could not look. `isError: false` plus an empty array means it looked and found nothing.

steps.title: Two empty arrays, two meanings
steps.lead: One tool, one return shape, two completely different realities behind it.

ask.q: A `get_customer` tool returns an empty array both when no customer matches the search and when the customer database is unreachable. The agent retries on both and eventually escalates with "customer not found." Which approach is most effective?
options: Return `isError: true` whenever the results array is empty, so the agent always escalates rather than guessing.
Return `isError: false` with an empty array when no customer matches, and `isError: true` with `errorCategory: "transient"` and `isRetryable: true` when the database is unreachable.
Increase the retry count and raise the timeout so transient database failures resolve on their own.
When the result is empty, have the agent ask the user to confirm their customer ID before proceeding.
ask.why: A valid empty result is information, not an error, so `isError: false` with an empty array lets the agent say no customer was found, while a real access failure carries `isError: true` with a transient category so the agent can decide whether to retry. Always escalating mislabels a success, more retries cannot repair a misclassified empty result, and asking the user to confirm an ID that does not exist burns a turn on a non-problem.

steps.takeaway: Separate access failure from valid empty in the contract, not in the agent's prose.

steps.title: Four categories, four next moves
steps.lead: Every failure should answer three questions the agent actually needs: what happened, can retrying help, and what was attempted.
points: `transient`: timeout, 503, rate limit. Retryable, and retry with the same input.
`validation`: bad format, missing field, malformed ID. Retryable only after the agent fixes the input.
`business`: policy limit exceeded, account locked, not eligible. Never retryable, and it carries a customer-friendly description.
`permission`: 401, 403, missing scope. Never retryable, so the agent escalates.
A write that times out after submission is an uncertain outcome, not a retry. Protocol errors mean the request never ran.
steps.takeaway: The error contract is the recovery signal. "Operation failed" strips exactly the information the decision needs.

steps.title: What reaches the coordinator
steps.lead: A subagent fails mid-task. What it hands upward decides whether the workflow survives.
points: The subagent recovers locally first, one or two retries, capped.
Only what it cannot resolve travels up, carrying failure type, the attempted query, `attempted_action`, and `partial_results`.
The coordinator evaluates partial results and retries, reroutes, or annotates the gap. It does not abort on one subagent failure.
steps.caption: Only unresolved failures travel upward, and they travel with context.
steps.takeaway: Partial progress beats a clean abort.

steps.title: Reliability fails before the context window does
steps.lead: One agent, eighteen tools, wrong selection. Its task mix genuinely requires all eighteen capabilities.
points: Cap each agent at four or five role-relevant tools and distribute the rest across specialized subagents.
Scope tools to roles: a synthesis agent gets no web search, a search agent gets no document analysis.
Expanding all eighteen descriptions does not change the count, and the count is the failure.
`tool_choice: "any"` forces a tool call. It does not force a specific tool.
High-frequency simple cross-role need: ship a constrained tool with an escalation boundary, e.g. `verify_fact(claim, max_sources=3)`.
steps.takeaway: Tool count and tool scope are architecture, not style. Four or five per agent.

steps.title: Eighteen tools is the failure
steps.lead: A capability count problem is being misdiagnosed as a wording problem.

ask.q: One agent has 18 tools configured and frequently selects the wrong one. Its task mix genuinely requires all 18 capabilities. Which approach is most effective?
options: Expand all 18 tool descriptions with I/O contracts, examples, and explicit boundaries.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` so the model must commit to a tool rather than answering in text.
Distribute the tools across specialized subagents, giving each 4-5 role-relevant tools.
Add few-shot selection examples for all 18 tools to the system prompt.
ask.why: Selection reliability degrades with the number of tools in front of the model, and each subagent should carry only its role-relevant set. Better descriptions do not change the count, `tool_choice: "any"` forces a call without improving which one, and examples for 18 tools add token cost on every request while leaving the overload in place.

steps.takeaway: Eighteen well-described tools are still eighteen tools.

steps.title: Prompts request, tool_choice requires
steps.lead: A support flow must always call `extract_intent` before routing. It is written as mandatory in the system prompt, and about 15% of turns skip it.
points: A prompt instruction is probabilistic. `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_intent"}` is structural.
Force the value on the first turn, then switch to `"auto"` for the rest.
`"any"` guarantees a tool call. It does not guarantee the right tool. `"none"` returns prose with the tools still declared.
Constraining capability at the interface makes the wrong behaviour impossible rather than discouraged.
Constrained replacements: `fetch_url(url)` becomes `load_document(document_url)`; `run_sql(query)` becomes `query_orders(filters)`.
steps.takeaway: A prompt cannot deliver a deterministic guarantee. `tool_choice` can.

steps.title: Making the first call mandatory
steps.lead: The instruction is already imperative and it still fails one turn in seven.

ask.q: Every customer message must call `extract_intent` before routing, and today that is enforced by a system prompt instruction. About 15% of messages skip the extraction step. Which approach is most effective?
options: Set `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_intent"}` on the first turn, then switch to `"auto"` for subsequent turns.
Strengthen the system prompt to state that intent extraction is mandatory before routing.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the first turn so the model must call some tool.
Add a post-hoc validation step that re-runs routing whenever the extraction output is missing.
ask.why: A forced tool choice makes the first call structurally guaranteed where a prompt only makes it probable. `"any"` still lets the model pick a different tool, stronger prose is the same probabilistic mechanism that already failed 15% of the time, and post-hoc validation pays for a second pass after the wrong action may already have been taken.

steps.takeaway: For must-call-X-first, reach for `tool_choice`, not a louder instruction.

steps.title: Scope decides who gets the integration
steps.lead: Six developers, one GitHub MCP server, one personal token each. You want the same tooling everywhere and no credential in the repository.
points: Team-shared servers go in project scope: `.mcp.json` at the repo root, version-controlled.
Personal and experimental servers go in `~/.claude.json` as user scope.
Reference secrets with `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` expansion and document the variable for onboarding. Never commit the value.
When a token leaks, parameterise it and rotate it. Never relocate the file or gitignore `.mcp.json`; that ends team sharing.
On a name collision the precedence is local, then project, then user. The whole entry wins, fields are not merged.
steps.takeaway: Project scope for the team, user scope for the individual, `${VAR}` for every secret.

steps.title: Six developers, one token each
steps.lead: The requirement is shared tooling plus per-developer credentials.

ask.q: Your team wants to add a GitHub MCP server for searching PRs and checking CI status in Claude Code. Six developers each have a personal GitHub token. You want consistent tooling across the team without committing credentials. Which approach is most effective?
options: Have each developer add the server in user scope with `claude mcp add --scope user`.
Create an MCP server wrapper that reads tokens from a `.env` file and proxies GitHub API calls, then add the wrapper to the project `.mcp.json`.
Configure the server in project scope with a placeholder token and tell developers to override it in local config.
Add the server to the project `.mcp.json` using environment variable substitution (`${GITHUB_TOKEN}`) for auth, and document the required variable in the project README.
ask.why: A version-controlled `.mcp.json` with `${VAR}` expansion gives one shared source of truth for the configuration while each developer supplies their own secret locally. User-scope setup loses the shared source of truth, a custom proxy is unnecessary engineering when built-in expansion already exists, and a committed placeholder token risks accidental use.

steps.takeaway: Shared file, personal secret. `${VAR}` expansion is the mechanism that already exists.

steps.title: Resources show, tools act
steps.lead: A support agent opens every conversation with a dozen exploratory calls to work out what data the backend exposes. Context is gone before real work starts.
points: Expose MCP resources as catalogues: schemas, issue summaries, content listings. The agent reads the catalogue once, then queries precisely.
Resources are what is true and stable about a system. Tools are the actions on it.
For a standard integration, adopt the maintained community server first, then post-process it or fork it rather than building from scratch.
When a capable MCP tool keeps losing to a built-in, strengthen the MCP tool's description. Do not delete the built-in.
MCP annotations such as `readOnlyHint` are untrusted hints, never a security boundary.
steps.takeaway: Catalogue with a resource, act with a tool.

steps.title: MCP is a hub, not a pipe
steps.lead: One client, several servers, each declaring its own surface.
points: Server primitives: tools are model-controlled, resources are application-controlled, prompts are user-driven.
Lifecycle runs `initialize`, then `notifications/initialized`, then `tools/list`, then `tools/call`, over JSON-RPC 2.0.
A `url` with no `type` is skipped with a warning, so always set the transport type explicitly.
steps.caption: One client, many servers, each announcing what it offers before anything is called.
steps.takeaway: Know what a server exposes before you call it.

steps.title: Grep finds content, Glob finds paths
steps.lead: You need every caller of `legacyAuth`, and then the test files that cover those callers. Each test file is the source name with a `.test.ts` suffix.
points: Grep searches file contents and returns matching lines: callers, identifiers, error strings, imports.
Glob matches file paths and returns paths: extensions and name patterns such as `**/*.test.ts`.
The order depends on which one is the seed. Content-seeded means Grep first, then Glob to narrow paths around the result.
Path-seeded is the mirror: you already know the file set, so Glob first and Grep to check contents.
Asking which files exist is a path question, so Glob. Grepping `import React` to find components is the wrong direction.
steps.takeaway: Grep is contents, Glob is paths. Find the seed, then filter with the other.

steps.title: Edit needs a unique anchor
steps.lead: An Edit fails with multiple matches: the snippet you targeted appears identically in six places, and only one should change.
points: The ladder is fixed. First widen `old_string` with surrounding context until the match is unique.
If no unique anchor exists at all, Read the whole file and Write the corrected version.
`replace_all: true` is only for the case where every occurrence really should change.
A shell text tool is the wrong category, and so is deleting and rewriting the file.
Build understanding incrementally: Grep entry points, Read those, Grep the identifiers you found. Never read every file upfront.
steps.takeaway: Edit fails structurally, not semantically. Widen the anchor before you change tools.

steps.title: Six identical matches, one target
steps.lead: The tool is working correctly. The anchor is the problem.

ask.q: An Edit call fails with "multiple matches": the target snippet appears identically in six places in a 400-line config, and only one occurrence should change. Which approach is most effective?
options: Run `sed -i` over the file to replace the target string.
Expand `old_string` with surrounding context until it is unique; if no unique anchor exists at all, Read the full file and Write the corrected version.
Set `replace_all: true` so the edit applies to every occurrence.
Delete the file and Write it again from scratch.
ask.why: Edit's failure mode is structural, because it needs a unique anchor, so the first move is to widen the anchor with Read-then-Write as the fallback when nothing unique exists. A shell text tool is the wrong category, `replace_all` rewrites five sites that should not change, and deleting the file is destructive and loses content.

steps.takeaway: A non-unique match is an anchor problem, not a tool problem.

steps.title: Names change at the module boundary
steps.lead: `formatDate` is defined in `date.ts` and re-exported from `index.ts` as `formatDateISO`. Grepping only the original name finds the definition and misses the production callers.
points: Read the wrapper module first and list what it exports.
Note every alias the export renames the original identifier to.
Grep each alias across the codebase, not just the origin name.
Grepping the import path finds the module boundary, not the call sites.
steps.caption: One definition, two names, and only one of them appears at the call sites.
steps.takeaway: Grep the alias, not the origin. The original name misses alias callers.

steps.title: Domain 2 in one page
steps.lead: That is Domain 2. Five tasks, one chain: the description routes the call, the schema constrains the arguments, the error contract decides recovery, scope decides who can call it, and built-in choice decides what the work costs. This is the spine.
points: Descriptions are the routing layer, not documentation. Fix order: descriptions, few-shot, merge, routing classifier, which is wrong.
An "or" or a "depending on" inside a description means split the tool. Renaming and enums do not fix it.
`isError: true` means the tool could not look. `isError: false` with an empty array means it looked and found nothing.
Transient retries the same input; validation after a fix; business and permission never retry. Post-submission timeouts are uncertainty.
Four or five role-relevant tools per agent. Must-do-X-first is `tool_choice` with a named tool, never a prompt.
Team servers live in project `.mcp.json` with `${VAR}`; personal ones in `~/.claude.json`. Precedence: local, project, user.
Expose MCP resources as catalogues. When an MCP tool loses to a built-in, fix the description, do not remove the built-in.
Grep is contents, Glob is paths. Edit needs a unique anchor; widen it before reaching for Read and Write.
steps.takeaway: Every Domain 2 stem asks the same thing: which layer fixes this, and is it the cheapest one that reaches the root cause?
